summary: Defines a portion of the MIB for managing the Border Gateway Protocol version 3. It was replaced by RFC 4273.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a checklist for monitoring routers that use BGP.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for Border Gateway Protocol version 3

tldr.problem: BGP routers needed a standard way to be monitored and managed using SNMP, allowing operators to see the status of inter-domain routing connections and path information.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines managed objects for BGP system variables, peer connections, and received path attributes. It provides read-only access to peer state and statistics, and read-write access to administrative controls.
tldr.outcome: This enables monitoring of BGP routing across autonomous systems. It was later replaced by RFC 4273 with updated definitions based on BGP version 4.

today: RFC 1269 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 4273, which provides updated definitions for BGP-4 and includes improvements based on operational experience.

sections.title: BGP Management Through SNMP
sections.content:
RFC 1269 defines the Management Information Base (MIB) for the Border Gateway Protocol version 3 (BGP-3). BGP is an inter-domain routing protocol used to exchange network reachability information between Autonomous Systems on the Internet. This RFC provides SNMP-based management capability for BGP implementations.

BGP runs over a reliable transport protocol (TCP), which eliminates the need for many reliability mechanisms at the BGP layer. The protocol can use authentication schemes from the underlying transport protocol. This RFC focuses on providing visibility and control of BGP peer connections and the routing path information they exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP is how different internet providers tell each other about the networks they handle. This document is the rulebook for monitoring those conversations.

sections.title: BGP Peer Connections and Path Attributes
sections.content:
The BGP MIB is organized around two main concepts: BGP peer connections and the path attributes they exchange. A BGP peer is another BGP-speaking router that this system exchanges routing information with. The Peer Table reflects information about BGP peer connections, such as their state and current activity.

The Received Path Attribute Table contains all attributes received from all peers before local routing policy has been applied. These path attributes describe how to reach destination networks, including the sequence of Autonomous Systems that must be traversed, the origin of the route information, and the next-hop address to use.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP peers are routers that talk to each other. The MIB tracks what each peer is doing and what routing information each one has sent.

sections.title: BGP System Variables and Peer States
sections.content:
The MIB defines several system-level objects that describe the BGP implementation itself. The BGP version object indicates which versions of the BGP protocol are supported. The local autonomous system number identifies this system on the internet. The BGP identifier is the router ID used in BGP connections.

Each BGP peer connection is tracked through the Peer Table, which records the peer's IP address and autonomous system number, the connection state (idle, connect, active, opensent, openconfirm, or established), the negotiated BGP version, the local and remote TCP ports used, and statistics on the number of UPDATE messages and total messages exchanged. The table also records the last error seen on the connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The system variables tell you which BGP versions the router speaks and its AS number. The Peer Table shows what state each peer connection is in and how many messages have been sent.

sections.title: Path Attributes and Route Information
sections.content:
Path attributes are the core of BGP routing information. Each received path is indexed by the destination network and the peer that provided it. The origin attribute indicates whether the route came from an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP), an Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), or is of undetermined origin.

The AS Path attribute contains the sequence of Autonomous Systems that must be traversed to reach the destination network. It is represented as pairs of octets, with each pair encoding one AS number. The next-hop address tells the router which border gateway to send traffic toward for this destination. The inter-AS metric, when present, provides an optional metric for route selection.
sections.plainLanguage: When a BGP peer sends route information, it tells you the destination network, which routers' domains the traffic has to pass through, and which router to send it to first.

sections.title: Management Framework and Notifications
sections.content:
This MIB follows the Internet-standard Network Management Framework defined by RFC 1155 (SMI), RFC 1213 (MIB-II), and RFC 1157 (SNMP). All objects are defined using the standard SNMP conventions and can be accessed by any SNMP management application.

The RFC defines two SNMP traps (notifications) for BGP events: the BGP Established trap is sent when a BGP peer connection transitions to the ESTABLISHED state, and the BGPBackwardTransition trap is sent when the peer connection moves from a higher-numbered state to a lower-numbered state (indicating a failure or reset). These traps allow management stations to be immediately notified of significant BGP state changes.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB uses the same standards that all internet network management uses. It can also send alarm messages when important things happen with BGP peer connections.
